articleHeadline: In a drier world, some infectious diseases are unexpectedly thriving
articleSummary: Drought-disease paradox: a hotter, drier world can fuel certain infections. articleSummary: Russian flu (1889) was the first modern pandemic, spreading globally at high speed via rail and steamships. Originating in May 1889 in Bukhara (present-day Uzbekistan) under the Russian Empire, it reached Saint Petersburg and Moscow by October, Berlin and Paris shortly after, and by December crossed the Atlantic to New York, with later reach to Buenos Aires, India, and Australia. About 60% of residents in major cities were infected and roughly 1 million people died worldwide. Essential workers—postmen, telegraph operators, tram drivers, bankers—were hit first due to extensive contact and handling mail and goods from infected areas. Symptoms included high fever, cough, rashes, GI issues, extreme fatigue, and loss of taste and smell; the mortality curve was J-shaped, heavily affecting the elderly. The etiologic agent remains uncertain (influenza A subtypes vs coronavirus) due to lack of preserved tissue samples. Public health impact included the first use of excess mortality to quantify impact and the recognition that borders do not stop pathogens.

articleHeadline: Geospatial tools help track Ebola and prevent spread
articleSummary: Ebola outbreaks in eastern DRC are analyzed with geospatial intelligence. Earth observation—satellite imagery, environmental monitoring, mobility data and geospatial analysis—supplements epidemiological surveillance in North Kivu and Ituri where conflict and displacement disrupt health services. Preparedness benefits from monitoring forest fragmentation, land use and urban encroachment to target surveillance before crises. During outbreaks, high-resolution imagery identifies settlements, roads, health facilities and population distribution, while epidemiology clarifies where disease exists and how environment and social factors influence spread. Mongbwalu imagery documents post-attack disruptions to temporary medical facilities, illustrating operational impact. Mobility models estimate travel times to treatment centers and identify underserved populations. The aim is a public health intelligence system—integrating Earth observation, surveillance, conflict data, mobility, accessibility and local knowledge—demonstrated by Servir with Liberia’s 2014–16 Ebola epidemic and South Sudan preparedness.

The system would monitor respiratory infections (influenza, COVID-19, RSV, tuberculosis) and febrile syndromes (malaria, bacteremia, typhoid). articleSummary: Nature Communications reports a deep learning approach to precision grading of liver fibrosis caused by Schistosoma japonicum, using ultrasound images.
